newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace to challenge UK govt in court over oil.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace to challenge UK govt in court over oil.

text.p: Greenpeace is seeking to take the British Government to court this week over plans to open up Atlantic waters for oil exploration, the environmental group said on Monday.
"We intend to lodge papers sometime this week to ask leave from the High Court to pursue the case," said Greenpeace spokesperson Mirella Lindenfels.

She said the campaign group believed the government had failed to apply the European Habitats Directive when it awarded permits in the 17th offshore licensing round for oil exploration, mainly in the Rockall Trough west of the Hebrides and north of the Shetland Islands earlier this year.

In an unprecedented move back in March Greenpeace applied for all the licenses with the intention of turning the 22,000 square miles into a marine wildlife sanctuary. The bid was rejected by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and the licenses were granted to 14 oil companies.
If the High Court grants Greenpeace leave the case will go to court and the group said it will call for the oil exploration to be suspended until the case is concluded.
The DTI rejection of the Greenpeace license bid heralded the start of concerted campaigning.
Earlier this month activists occupied the London office of U.S. oil company Conoco, which among others was awarded the right to explore for oil in the 17th licensing round, for about four hours.

A week ago Greenpeace campaigners seized the tiny, barren Atlantic Island of Rockall and rejecting British claims proclaimed a new state of Waveland. The declaration of a new state was aimed at protecting the Atlantic Frontier from oil exploration, the group said.

The latest twist, which Greenpeace hopes will result in the case going to court, was prompted after the DTI responded in an "unsatisfactory" way to a Greenpeace letter threatening legal action said the group's Lindenfels.
A spokesman for the Department of Trade and Industry said the government's position had been laid out in a letter sent to Greenpeace on June 18.
"It goes without saying, if we have to go to court then we will," the spokesman said.
